entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1-1Sam.9.2">1Sa 9:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">Saul searches for his father’s asses</hi>. - <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1Sa 9:1</reference>, 1Sa 9:2. The elaborate genealogy of the Benjaminite Kish, and the minute description of the figure of his son Saul, are intended to indicate at the very outset the importance to which Saul attained in relation to the people of Israel, <hi type="italic">Kish</hi> was the son of <hi type="italic">Abiel</hi>: this is in harmony with 1Sa 14:51. But when, on the other hand, it is stated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33">1Ch 8:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.39">1Ch 9:39</reference>, that <hi type="italic">Ner</hi> begat <hi type="italic">Kish</hi>, the difference may be reconciled in the simplest manner, on the assumption that the <hi type="italic">Ner</hi> mentioned there is not the father, but the grandfather, or a still more remote ancestor of Kish, as the intervening members are frequently passed over in the genealogies. The other ancestors of <hi type="italic">Kish</hi> are never mentioned again. חיל גּבּור refers to <hi type="italic">Kish</hi>, and signifies not a brave man, but a man of property, as in Rth 2:1. This son <hi type="italic">Saul</hi> (i.e., “<hi type="italic">prayed for</hi>:” for this meaning of the word, comp. <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.17">1Sa 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.27">1Sa 1:27</reference>) was “<hi type="italic">young and beautiful</hi>.” It is true that even at that time Saul had a son grown up (viz., Jonathan), according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.2">1Sa 13:2</reference>; but still, in contrast with his father, he was “a young man,” i.e., in the full vigour of youth, probably about forty or forty-five years old. There is no necessity, therefore, to follow the Vulgate rendering <hi type="italic">electus</hi>. No one equalled him in beauty. “<hi type="italic">From his shoulder upwards he was higher than any of the people</hi>.” Such a figure as this was well adapted to commend him to the people as their king (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.24">1Sa 10:24</reference>), since size and beauty were highly valued in rulers, as signs of manly strength (see Herod. iii. 20, vii. 187; Aristot. <hi type="italic">Polit</hi>. iv. c. 24).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.3-1Sam.9.5">1Sa 9:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen3767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3768" type="x-p"/> Having been sent out by his father to search for his she-asses which had strayed, Saul went with his servant through the mountains of Ephraim, which ran southwards into the tribe-territory of Benjamin (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.1">1Sa 1:1</reference>), then through the land of Shalishah and the land of Shaalim, and after that through the land of Benjamin, without finding the asses; and at length, when he had reached the land of Zuph, he determined to return, because he was afraid that his father might turn his mind from the asses, and trouble himself about them (the son and servant). מן חדל, to desist from a thing, to give it up or renounce it. <div eID="gen3768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3769" type="x-p"/> As Saul started in any case from Gibeah of Benjamin, his own home (1Sa 10:10., <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.26">1Sa 10:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.4">1Sa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.34">1Sa 15:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1Sa 23:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1">1Sa 26:1</reference>), i.e., the present <hi type="italic">Tuleil el Phul</hi>, which was an hour or an hour and a half to the north of Jerusalem (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.28">Jos 18:28</reference>), and went thence into the mountains of Ephraim, he no doubt took a north-westerly direction, so that he crossed the boundary of Benjamin somewhere between Bireh and Atarah, and passing through the crest of the mountains of Ephraim, on the west of Gophnah (Jifna), came out into the land of Shalishah. <hi type="italic">Shalishah</hi> is unquestionably the country round (or of) <hi type="italic">Baal-shalishah</hi> (2Ki 4:42), which was situated, according to <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> (<hi type="italic">Onom. s.v</hi>. Βαιθσαρισάθ: <hi type="italic">Beth-sarisa</hi> or <hi type="italic">Beth-salisa</hi>), <hi type="italic">in regione Thamnitica</hi>, fifteen Roman miles to the north of Diospolis (Lydda), and was therefore probably the country to the west of Jiljilia, where three different wadys run into one large wady, called Kurawa; and according to the probable conjecture of Thenius, it was from this fact that the district received the name of <hi type="italic">Shalishah</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Three-land</hi>. They proceeded thence in their search to the land of <hi type="italic">Shaalim</hi>: according to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. (<hi type="italic">s.v.</hi>), “a village seven miles off, <hi type="italic">in finibus Eleutheropoleos contra occidentem</hi>.” But this is hardly correct, and is most likely connected with the mistake made in transposing the town of Samuel to the neighbourhood of Diospolis (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.1">1Sa 1:1</reference>). For since they went on from Shaalim into the land of Benjamin, and then still further into the land of Zuph, on the south-west of Benjamin, they probably turned eastwards from Shalishah, into the country where we find <hi type="italic">Beni Mussah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Beni Salem</hi> marked upon <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>'s and v. de Velde’s maps, and where we must therefore look for the land of <hi type="italic">Shaalim</hi>, that they might proceed thence to explore the land of Benjamin from the north-east to the south-west. If, on the contrary, they had gone from Shaalim in a southerly or south-westerly direction, to the district of Eleutheropolis, they would only have entered the land of Benjamin at the south-west corner, and would have had to go all the way back again in order to go thence to the land of Zuph. For we may infer with certainty that the land of Zuph was on the south-west of the tribe-territory of Benjamin, from the fact that, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>, Saul and his companion passed Rachel’s tomb on their return thence to their own home, and then came to the border of Benjamin. On the name <hi type="italic">Zuph</hi>, see at 1Sa 1:1.

1Sa 9:3-5

As Saul started in any case from Gibeah of Benjamin, his own home (1Sa 10:10., 1Sa 10:26 , 1Sa 11:4 ; 1Sa 15:34 ; 1Sa 23:19 ; 1Sa 26:1 ), i.e., the present Tuleil el Phul , which was an hour or an hour and a half to the north of Jerusalem (see at Jos 18:28 ), and went thence into the mountains of Ephraim, he no doubt took a north-westerly direction, so that he crossed the boundary of Benjamin somewhere between Bireh and Atarah, and passing through the crest of the mountains of Ephraim, on the west of Gophnah (Jifna), came out into the land of Shalishah. Shalishah is unquestionably the country round (or of) Baal-shalishah (2Ki 4:42), which was situated, according to Eusebius ( Onom. s.v . Βαιθσαρισάθ: Beth-sarisa or Beth-salisa ), in regione Thamnitica , fifteen Roman miles to the north of Diospolis (Lydda), and was therefore probably the country to the west of Jiljilia, where three different wadys run into one large wady, called Kurawa; and according to the probable conjecture of Thenius, it was from this fact that the district received the name of Shalishah , or Three-land . They proceeded thence in their search to the land of Shaalim : according to the Onom . ( s.v. ), “a village seven miles off, in finibus Eleutheropoleos contra occidentem .” But this is hardly correct, and is most likely connected with the mistake made in transposing the town of Samuel to the neighbourhood of Diospolis (see at 1Sa 1:1 ). For since they went on from Shaalim into the land of Benjamin, and then still further into the land of Zuph, on the south-west of Benjamin, they probably turned eastwards from Shalishah, into the country where we find Beni Mussah and Beni Salem marked upon Robinson 's and v. de Velde’s maps, and where we must therefore look for the land of Shaalim , that they might proceed thence to explore the land of Benjamin from the north-east to the south-west. If, on the contrary, they had gone from Shaalim in a southerly or south-westerly direction, to the district of Eleutheropolis, they would only have entered the land of Benjamin at the south-west corner, and would have had to go all the way back again in order to go thence to the land of Zuph. For we may infer with certainty that the land of Zuph was on the south-west of the tribe-territory of Benjamin, from the fact that, according to 1Sa 10:2 , Saul and his companion passed Rachel’s tomb on their return thence to their own home, and then came to the border of Benjamin. On the name Zuph , see at 1Sa 1:1.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6">1Sa 9:6</reference> <div eID="gen3769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3770" type="x-p"/> When Saul proposed to return home from the land of Zuph, his servant said to him, “<hi type="italic">Behold, in this city</hi> (<hi type="italic">'this</hi>,' referring to the town which stood in front of them upon a hill) <hi type="italic">is a man of God, much honoured; all that he saith cometh surely to pass: now we will go thither; perhaps he will tell us our way that we have to go</hi>” (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. have gone, and still go, sc., to attain the object of our journey, viz., to find the asses). The name of this town is not mentioned either here or in the further course of this history. Nearly all the commentators suppose it to have been Ramah, Samuel’s home. But this assumption has no foundation at all in the text, and is irreconcilable with the statements respecting the return in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>-5. The servant did not say there <hi type="italic">dwells</hi> in this city, but there is in this city (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6">1Sa 9:6</reference>; comp. with this <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.10">1Sa 9:10</reference>, “They went into the city where the man of God was,” not “dwelt”). It is still more evident, from the answer given by the drawers of water, when Saul asked them, “<hi type="italic">Is the seer here?</hi>” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.11">1Sa 9:11</reference>), - viz., “<hi type="italic">He came to-day to the city, for the people have a great sacrifice upon the high place</hi>” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.12">1Sa 9:12</reference>), - that the seer (Samuel) did not live in the town, but had only come thither to a sacrificial festival. Moreover, “every impartial man will admit, that the fact of Samuel’s having honoured Saul as his guest at the sacrificial meal of those who participated in the sacrifice, and of their having slept under the same roof, cannot possibly weaken the impression that Samuel was only there in his peculiar and official capacity. It could not be otherwise than that the presidency should be assigned to him at the feast itself as priest and prophet, and therefore that the appointments mentioned should proceed from him. And it is but natural to assume that he had a house at his command for any repetition of such sacrifices, which we find from 2 Kings 4 to have been the case in the history of Elisha” (Valentiner). And lastly, the sacrificial festival itself does not point to Ramah; for although Samuel had built an altar to the Lord at Ramah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.17">1Sa 7:17</reference>), this was by no means the only place of sacrifice in the nation. If Samuel offered sacrifice at Mizpeh and Gilgal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.9">1Sa 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.8">1Sa 10:8</reference>; 1Sa 13:8.), he could also do the same at other places. What the town really was in which Saul met with him, cannot indeed be determined, since all that we can gather from <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>, is, that it was situated on the south-west of Bethlehem.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.9-1Sam.9.10">1Sa 9:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen3771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3772" type="x-p"/> Before proceeding with the further progress of the affair, the historian introduces a notice, which was required to throw light upon what follows; namely, that beforetime, if any one wished to inquire of God, i.e., to apply to a prophet for counsel from God upon any matter, it was customary in Israel to say, We will go to the seer, because “<hi type="italic">he that is now called a prophet was beforetime called a seer</hi>.” After this parenthetical remark, the account is continued in 1Sa 9:10. Saul declared himself satisfied with the answer of the servant; and they both went into the town, to ask the man of God about the asses that were lost.

entries.reader_content_plain:
1Sa 9:11-12
As they were going up to the high place of the town, they met maidens coming out of the town to draw water; and on asking them whether the seer was there, they received this answer: “ Yes; behold, he is before thee: make haste, now, for he has come into the town to-day; for the people have a sacrifice to-day upon the high place .” Bamah (in the singular) does not mean the height or hill generally; but throughout it signifies the high place , as a place of sacrifice or prayer.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.13">1Sa 9:13</reference> <div eID="gen3773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3774" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">When ye come into the city, ye will find him directly before he goes up to the high place to eat</hi>.” כּן not only introduces the apodosis, but corresponds to כּ, <hi type="italic">as</hi>, so: here, however, it is used with reference to time, in the sense of our “immediately.” “<hi type="italic">For the people are not accustomed to eat till he comes, for he blesses the sacrifice</hi>,” etc. בּרך, like εὐλογεῖν, refers to the thanksgiving prayer offered before the sacrificial meal. “<hi type="italic">Go now for him; yet will meet him even to-day</hi>.” The first אתו is placed at the beginning for the sake of emphasis, and then repeated at the close. כּהיּום, “<hi type="italic">Even to-day</hi>.”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.14-1Sam.9.16">1Sa 9:14-16</reference> <div eID="gen3774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3775" type="x-p"/> When they went into the town, Samuel met them on his way out to go to the high place of sacrifice. Before the meeting itself is described, the statement is introduced in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15-1Sam.9.17">1Sa 9:15-17</reference>, that the day before Jehovah had foretold to Samuel that the man was coming to him whom he was to anoint as captain over his people. אזן גּלה, to <hi type="italic">open any one’s ear</hi>, equivalent to <hi type="italic">reveal</hi> something to him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12">1Sa 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.27">2Sa 7:27</reference>, etc.). אשׁלח, <hi type="italic">I will send thee</hi>, i.e., “I will so direct his way in my overruling providence, that he shall come to thee” (J. H. Mich. ). The words, “<hi type="italic">that he may save my people out of the hand of the Philistines; for I have looked upon my people, for their cry is come unto me</hi>,” are not at all at variance with 1Sa 7:13. In that passage there is simply the assertion, that there was no more any permanent oppression on the part of the Philistines in the days of Samuel, such as had taken place before; but an attempt to recover their supremacy over Israel is not only not precluded, but is even indirectly affirmed (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.13">1Sa 7:13</reference>). The words before us simply show that the Philistines had then begun to make a fresh attempt to contend for dominion over the Israelites. “<hi type="italic">I have looked upon my people</hi>:” this is to be explained like the similar passage in <reference osisRef="Exod.2.25">Exo 2:25</reference>, “God looked upon the children of Israel,” and <reference osisRef="Exod.3.7">Exo 3:7</reference>, “I have looked upon the misery of my people.” God’s looking was not a quiet, inactive looking on, but an energetic look, which brought help in trouble. “<hi type="italic">Their cry is come unto me</hi>:” this is word for word the same as in Exo 3:9. As the Philistines wanted to tread in the footsteps of the Egyptians, it was necessary that Jehovah should also send His people a deliverer from these new oppressors, by giving them a king. The reason here assigned for the establishment of a monarchy is by no means at variance with the displeasure which God had expressed to Samuel at the desire of the people for a king (1Sa 8:7.); since this displeasure had reference to the state of heart from which the desire had sprung.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.18-1Sam.9.24">1Sa 9:18-24</reference> <div eID="gen3776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3777" type="x-p"/> The thread of the narrative, which was broken off in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15">1Sa 9:15</reference>, is resumed in 1Sa 9:18. Saul drew near to Samuel in the gate, and asked him for the seer’s house. The expression השּׁער בּתוך is used to define more precisely the general phrase in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.14">1Sa 9:14</reference>, העיר בּתוך בּאים; and there is no necessity to alter העיר in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.14">1Sa 9:14</reference> into השּׁער, as Thenius proposes, for העיר בּתוך כּוא does not mean to go (or be) in the middle of the town, as he imagines, but to go <hi type="italic">into</hi>, or enter, <hi type="italic">the town</hi>; and the entrance to the town was through the gate.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.25-1Sam.9.27">1Sa 9:25-27</reference> <div eID="gen3780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3781" type="x-p"/> When the sacrificial meal was over, Samuel and Saul went down from the high place into the town, and he (Samuel) talked with him upon the roof (of the house into which Samuel had entered). The flat roofs of the East were used as placed of retirement for private conversation (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.22.8">Deu 22:8</reference>). This conversation did not refer of course to the call of Samuel to the royal dignity, for that was not made known to him as a word of Jehovah till the following day (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.27">1Sa 9:27</reference>); but it was intended to prepare him for that announcement: so that <hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi>'s conjecture is probably the correct one, viz., that Samuel “talked with Saul concerning the deep religious and political degradation of the people of God, the oppression of the heathen, the causes of the inability of the Israelites to stand against these foes, the necessity for a conversion of the people, and the want of a leader who was entirely devoted to the Lord.”<note placement="foot">For הגּג על עם־שׁאוּל וידבּר the lxx have καὶ διέστρωσαν τῷ Σαοὺλ ἐπι τῷ δώματι καὶ ἐκοιμήθη, “they prepared Saul a bed upon the house, and he slept,” from which Clericus conjectured that these translators had read לשאול וירבדו (וירבּדוּ or ויּרבּדוּ); and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> and Thenius propose to alter the Hebrew text in this way. But although וגו ויּשׁכּימוּ (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.26">1Sa 9:26</reference>) no doubt presupposes that Saul had slept in Samuel’s house, and in fact upon the roof, the remark of Thenius, “that the private conversation upon the roof (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.25">1Sa 9:25</reference>) comes too early, as Saul did not yet know, and was not to learn till the following day, what was about to take place,” does not supply any valid objection to the correctness of the Masoretic text, or any argument in favour of the Septuagint rendering or interpretation, since it rests upon an altogether unfounded and erroneous assumption, viz., that Samuel had talked with Saul about his call to the throne. Moreover, “the strangeness” of the statement in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.26">1Sa 9:26</reference>, “they rose up early,” and then “when the morning dawned, Samuel called,” etc., cannot possibly throw any suspicion upon the integrity of the Hebrew text, as this “strangeness” vanishes when we take וגו כּעלות ויהי as a more precise definition of ויּשׁכּימוּ. The Septuagint translators evidently held the same opinion as their modern defenders. They took offence at Samuel’s private conversation with Saul, because he did not make known to him the word of God concerning his call to the throne till the next morning; and, on the other hand, as their rising the next morning is mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.26">1Sa 9:26</reference>, they felt the absence of any allusion to their sleeping, and consequently not only interpreted ידבר by a conjectural emendation as standing for ירבד rof, because מרבדּים רבד is used in <reference osisRef="Prov.7.16">Pro 7:16</reference> to signify the spreading of mats or carpets for a bed, but also identified וישׁכמו with ישׁכבו, and rendered it ἐκοιμήθη. At the same time, they did not reflect that the preparation of the bed and their sleeping during the night were both of them matters of course, and there was consequently no necessity to mention them; whereas Samuel’s talking with Saul upon the roof was a matter of importance in relation to the whole affair, and one which could not be passed over in silence. Moreover, the correctness of the Hebrew text is confirmed by all the other ancient versions. Not only do the Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic follow the Masoretic text, but <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> does the same in the rendering adopted by him, “<hi type="italic">Et locutus est cum Saule in solario. Cumque mane surrexissent;</hi>” though the words “<hi type="italic">stravitque Saul in solario et dormivit</hi>” have been interpolated probably from the Itala into the text of the Vulgate which has come down to us.</note>
